transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I'm here because everyone keeps acting like I'm just imagining it. But I know what I see. I know the hospital people and some of the folks from the agency have been watching our house. They've been following my cleaning routes, too, trying to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Which is just... it's insulting, really. I always do a thorough job, whether it's at home or at work. 

Like with my clients, I always go above and beyond. I had this one lady last week, Mrs. Gable, and she insisted I use this awful smelling pine cleaner on her expensive hardwood floors. I told her, you know, that's going to leave a terrible residue. I've been doing housekeeping for a long time, I know floors. But she just waved me off. People just don't respect the experience you bring to a job. I even brought my own microfiber mops because the ones she had were just pushing the dirt around into the corners. I found a really great deal on them at the hardware store downtown, the one next to the bakery that makes those little almond cookies my husband likes... 

Anyway, what did you ask me? Oh, right, why I came in. Yeah, they're watching my routes and the house, and I just need people to stop treating me like I'm making it up.
How long have you noticed people watching your house and following your work routes—did this start recently, or has it been going on for months or longer?

Well, it's been going on for a while now. I'd say about 11 months since I first noticed them watching us and, you know, hearing the voices talking about it. It started right around the time the weather started getting cold last year. I remember because I had just bought this beautiful wool coat from a second-hand shop on Elm Street. It was a steal, really, practically brand new, but it had this one loose button. I kept meaning to sew it back on, but you know how it is, you get busy with work and taking care of the house. 

My husband always tells me I need to slow down, but someone has to keep things organized. Like my cleaning caddy—if I don't organize it myself, the other girls at the agency just throw the sponges in with the glass cleaner, and that ruins them. Sponges are porous, you know, they absorb everything. You have to keep them separate. I actually found these great little waterproof bags online that work perfectly for that. They come in all these different colors... oh, but yes, it's been about 11 months of them watching and the voices.
You mentioned hearing voices talking about people watching you—can you describe what these voices sound like, such as whose voice it is and what they say to you?

Well, it's usually just one voice, mostly. It's a woman's voice. Even when the house is completely quiet, I'll hear her right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks or, you know, move my husband's pills. It's as clear as if she's standing right there next to the sink. 

Speaking of the sink, I really need to get a new drain stopper. The one we have is rubber, and it's getting that weird sticky feeling? You know how rubber gets when it breaks down? I tried scrubbing it with baking soda and a little vinegar—which is a great trick for hard water stains, by the way. I use it all the time at work. A lot of people think you need bleach for everything, but bleach is just too harsh. It ruins the grout in bathrooms if you use it too often. I tried telling that to my supervisor at the agency, but she just buys whatever is on sale in bulk. Last month she bought this terrible lemon-scented stuff that gave me a headache for two days straight. 

But anyway, yeah, she sounds like she's right there in the kitchen, telling me to check the locks and move the pills around.

Do you have any medical conditions—such as thyroid problems, seizures, head injuries, or other illnesses—or do you use alcohol or any recreational drugs, that started around the same time these voices and watching began?

Medical conditions? No, no, I'm healthy. No thyroid things or seizures or head injuries or anything like that. And I definitely don't do drugs or drink alcohol. I've seen enough of what alcohol does to people. 

Or, well, what it does to their houses, really. You wouldn't believe the messes people make when they've had a few drinks. Just a couple of months ago, I had this client, Mr. Henderson, who spilled a whole glass of red wine—I think it was a Merlot—right in the middle of his expensive cream-colored rug. And did he clean it up right away? Of course not. He just left it there overnight. You can't just rub a stain like that, you know, it pushes it right down into the fibers. You have to blot it gently. I always tell people, blot, don't rub! And use a little club soda, or even just regular table salt if it's fresh, to soak it up. 

But by the time I got there on Tuesday, it was completely dried in. People really think we housekeepers are just miracle workers who can turn back time. It's like when they leave soggy towels sitting on the hardwood floors. Wood warps, you know! You can't just let water sit on it. I had to use a special wood oil to fix this one spot near a bathtub once because the teenagers in the house had absolutely no respect for the flooring... but no, I don't have any medical problems or drink or anything.
Since these experiences began about 11 months ago, have you noticed any changes in your ability to keep up with your work, household responsibilities, or relationships with family and friends?

Well, it's been hard, honestly. My cleaning agency actually took away my supervisory routes. They said the clients and the other girls couldn't rely on my work the way they used to. Which is just ridiculous because I am the only one who knows how to properly clean a baseboard. You can't just swipe at it with a duster, you have to get down on your hands and knees with a damp microfiber cloth. Microfiber is really the best invention. It grabs all the dust instead of just pushing it around into the air. I buy the big packs of them from the hardware store, the yellow ones. 

But anyway, yeah, they took my routes. And at home, my husband and our pastor have had to step in a lot more. They say I'm not keeping up with everything safely, like the caregiving and the household chores. My husband tried doing the laundry last week, and he put my good silk blouse in the dryer. The dryer! I told him, you have to lay silk flat to dry, preferably on a clean, dry towel so it doesn't lose its shape. Heat just destroys the fibers. I spent an hour trying to steam the wrinkles out of it, but it's never going to be the same. I have this wonderful little handheld steamer, too, it heats up in thirty seconds. It's so much better than an iron for delicate things. But yes, things have definitely changed with my work and at home.

During these past 11 months, have you had any periods of feeling extremely sad, hopeless, or lacking energy, or on the other hand, unusually elated, energetic, or needing very little sleep, that lasted for a couple of weeks or more?

Well, sad? I don't know about extremely sad. Sometimes I get a little tired, I guess, but who doesn't? I haven't really had anything like that lasting for weeks. And I definitely haven't been bouncing off the walls or staying up all night. Sleep is very important. 

Speaking of sleep, you really have to wash your bedsheets in hot water to kill the dust mites. A lot of people wash their sheets in cold water to save energy, but cold water just doesn't get them truly clean. You need the heat. And you should never use fabric softener on towels or sheets. It leaves this waxy coating on them that makes them less absorbent. I learned that years ago when I first started cleaning for Mrs. Gable. She had these beautiful, thick Egyptian cotton towels, and she was complaining that they weren't drying her off properly. I took one look at her laundry room and saw three bottles of fabric softener lined up on the shelf. I told her, you have to use white vinegar in the rinse cycle instead. It naturally softens the fabric and gets rid of any soap residue. Plus, it cleans the washing machine at the same time! It's a win-win. 

But no, I haven't had any long periods of feeling super sad or overly energetic like you said. Just the normal amount of tired from dealing with everything.
Over these past 11 months, have you noticed yourself pulling away from friends, family, or activities you used to enjoy, or feeling less motivated or emotionally expressive than before?

Pulling away? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still go to church when I can, and I talk to my husband. I haven't lost my feelings or anything. I still get plenty fired up, especially when I see how some people treat their kitchens. 

Just last week, I was doing a deep clean for a new client, and I swear, they must have never wiped down the top of their kitchen cabinets. You know, the space between the cabinet and the ceiling? It was covered in this thick, sticky layer of grease and dust. People don't realize that when you cook, especially if you fry things, the grease travels up and settles on everything. You can't just use a regular all-purpose spray on that. It'll just smear it around. You have to use a good degreaser, something with citrus in it works best, or even just hot water and dish soap if you let it sit for a minute. And you have to use a scraper—gently, of course, so you don't scratch the wood finish. I spent an hour up on a step stool just working on those cabinets. It's really a hazard, all that grease. It attracts bugs, for one thing. Ants love a dirty kitchen. I always tell my clients, if you want to keep the ants away, you have to wipe down your counters every single night with a little bit of vinegar water. They hate the smell of vinegar. 

But no, I'm still myself. I haven't been hiding away or losing my motivation. I still care about doing a good job.

doctor.intent: Assess for negative symptoms of schizophrenia (e.g., social withdrawal, blunted affect, loss of motivation) to confirm the full symptom profile needed for the diagnosis
doctor.question: Over these past 11 months, have you noticed yourself pulling away from friends, family, or activities you used to enjoy, or feeling less motivated or emotionally expressive than before?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, blunted affect, asociality), which are not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Pulling away? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still go to church when I can, and I talk to my husband. I haven't lost my feelings or anything. I still get plenty fired up, especially when I see how some people treat their kitchens. 

Just last week, I was doing a deep clean for a new client, and I swear, they must have never wiped down the top of their kitchen cabinets. You know, the space between the cabinet and the ceiling? It was covered in this thick, sticky layer of grease and dust. People don't realize that when you cook, especially if you fry things, the grease travels up and settles on everything. You can't just use a regular all-purpose spray on that. It'll just smear it around. You have to use a good degreaser, something with citrus in it works best, or even just hot water and dish soap if you let it sit for a minute. And you have to use a scraper—gently, of course, so you don't scratch the wood finish. I spent an hour up on a step stool just working on those cabinets. It's really a hazard, all that grease. It attracts bugs, for one thing. Ants love a dirty kitchen. I always tell my clients, if you want to keep the ants away, you have to wipe down your counters every single night with a little bit of vinegar water. They hate the smell of vinegar. 

But no, I'm still myself. I haven't been hiding away or losing my motivation. I still care about doing a good job.

inference.note: Persecutory delusions, command auditory hallucinations, disorganized/tangential speech, and functional decline over 11 months, with no mood episode, substance use, or medical cause identified—supporting schizophrenia and ruling out mood disorder with psychosis, substance-induced psychosis, and medical/organic causes.
